reviews.evidence: The definition is the kernel of the sign map on S_n. Reading the target definitions confirms finite-permutation supplies S_n and permutation-sign supplies inversion-parity sign; kernel, group, and subgroup supply the construction and subgroup scope.

The finite-group class-size formula is orbit-stabilizer for the conjugation action: the class is the orbit and C_G(g) the stabilizer, whose index is computed. Conjugation-action is required with group, class, centralizer, index, and orbit-stabilizer.
The assignments A↦A/N and B↦π⁻¹(B) operate between subgroups of G and G/N. Quotient-group is a direct prerequisite alongside group, normal-subgroup, subgroup, and preimage.

The recursion uses commutator subgroups, while the core explicitly asserts each term is normal and each factor G^(n)/G^(n+1) is abelian. Group, commutator-subgroup, normal-subgroup, and quotient-group are all required.
The theorem’s actual hypotheses and conclusion concern integers, gcd, φ(n), and modular congruence. Group-of-units and Lagrange are only the proof route in Remarks and are not prerequisites.

The short exact sequence explicitly encodes injective and surjective maps, image/kernel equality, normal kernel, quotient identification, and isomorphisms. Group-isomorphism is required for the stated identifications.
Both displayed forms are arithmetic statements for an integer modulo a prime. The unit-group/Lagrange derivation is in Remarks and is not a defining input, so only integers remains.
The proposition assumes a finite cyclic group and constructs φ(k̄)=g^k as an isomorphism. Group, cyclic-subgroup, and group-isomorphism match the hypothesis, powers, and conclusion.
The core concludes with a unique group isomorphism G/ker(f)→im(f), making group-isomorphism an explicit output concept in addition to homomorphism, quotient, kernel, and image.
The theorem identifies the kernel as normal and induces an isomorphism from the quotient to the image. All six listed targets occur in the displayed statement and its surjective specialization.

The core defines X^G for a given group action as points fixed by every group element. Group-action is the sole defining prerequisite; stabilizer and center appear only in equivalent/examples sections.
The finite group G, normal subgroup N, Sylow p-subgroup P of N, and normalizer N_G(P) are explicit hypotheses and terms of G=NN_G(P). The four listed targets directly define them.
Freeness is defined by every stabilizer G_x being trivial. Group-action and stabilizer supply the action and fixed-point subgroup; regular-action is a later consequence only.
The universal property explicitly quantifies a set, functions i and f, groups, and a unique homomorphism. Function was added to the existing set, group, and homomorphism prerequisites.

The theorem assumes a finitely generated abelian group and displays a direct-sum decomposition. Abelian-group and direct-sum-groups supply exactly the hypothesis and construction; PID material is a remark.
The core defines ⟨S⟩ as an intersection of subgroups containing a subset S. Group, subset, intersection, and subgroup are all required for that displayed definition.
The core defines S generating G by ⟨S⟩=G. Group, subgroup, and generated-subgroup provide the ambient object, containment notion, and displayed construction.
An epimorphism is a group homomorphism that is surjective as a function. Those two listed targets state the complete definition; image/quotient occur in optional material.
The definition is a short exact sequence and explicitly identifies N as normal and Q canonically isomorphic to E/N. Group-isomorphism was added for that stated quotient identification.
A monomorphism is defined as a group homomorphism that is injective. The two listed targets exactly supply the definition; kernel/image are later equivalent-characterization consequences.
The displayed presentation is F(S) modulo the normal closure of R and requires S as a set. Free-group, normal-closure, quotient-group, and set directly support each construction.
The definition assumes a finite group and subgroup and sets gcd(|H|,[G:H])=1. Group, subgroup, index, and gcd are direct; Sylow/solvable material is explanatory context retained as linked content.

The core defines c_g(x)=gxg⁻¹ as an automorphism and Inn(G) as a subgroup of Aut(G). Group, automorphism-group, and subgroup supply the exact ambient and containment notions; quotient/center facts are later remarks.

The definition requires N,H subgroups, both normal, trivial intersection, and NH=G, then concludes the multiplication map is an isomorphism to a direct product. Intersection-of-subgroups was added for the explicit N∩H condition.
The definition requires N normal, N∩H={e}, NH=G, and uses conjugation H→Aut(N) to identify G with N⋊H. Intersection-of-subgroups was added for the explicit intersection condition.

The proposition defines the intersection of a family of subgroups and proves it is a subgroup, including the empty-intersection=G edge case. Group, subgroup, and set support the quantified family and construction.

The theorem assumes a group with a finite composition series and concludes equal lengths and isomorphic factor multisets. Composition-series, simple-group, and group-isomorphism supply the hypotheses and conclusion.

The core compares two composition series, explicitly quantifies quotient factors and an isomorphism permutation. Group-isomorphism was added for the displayed factor equivalences; quotient and simple-group support each factor.
The kernel is defined as the subgroup φ⁻¹({e_H}) of a homomorphism. Group-homomorphism and subgroup directly support the map and claimed subgroup; normality and quotient are remarks.
The proposition takes a homomorphism and its kernel and concludes normality. The three listed targets exactly supply map, kernel, and conjugation-invariant subgroup conclusion.
The core defines the action kernel as elements fixing every x. Group-action is the direct prerequisite; normality, permutation homomorphism, and faithfulness are consequences stated afterward.

The core proves a homomorphism kernel is normal. Homomorphism, kernel, and normal-subgroup are the only direct terms; quotient and first-isomorphism links are explanatory consequences. Integration classification: the reviewed current source includes a repair relative to the preceding validated commit.

The theorem assumes chain conditions on normal subgroups and compares direct-product decompositions into directly indecomposable factors, concluding isomorphism after permutation. Group, normal-subgroup, direct-product, and group-isomorphism match the statement.
The finite-group theorem partitions G into equal-cardinality cosets and states |G|=[G:H]|H|. Group, subgroup, coset, cardinality, partition, and index each occur in the displayed conclusion.

The definition combines an abelian group, partial order, lattice joins/meets, and translation invariance. The three listed targets provide precisely these structures; homomorphisms are a later morphism section.
The proposition defines g·x=gx and explicitly concludes the action is transitive and free, hence regular. Group, group-action, and regular-action are therefore all justified by the theorem statement.
A loop is defined as a quasigroup with an identity; the unique left/right division conditions are inherited from quasigroup and identity is stated locally. Quasigroup is the direct prerequisite.
The recursion defines γₙ₊₁=[γₙ,G] using the subgroup generated by explicit commutators. Group, commutator, and generated-subgroup supply the displayed construction; nilpotence examples are optional.
The core is exactly a set with a binary operation and no further axioms. Set and binary-operation directly provide both defining ingredients.
The theorem assumes a free group and subgroup, then gives freeness and, under finite rank/index, the formula rank(H)=1+[F:H](n−1). Free-group, subgroup, and index support the hypotheses and equation.

Nilpotence is defined by termination of the lower central series at {e}; group and lower-central-series are the direct defining prerequisites. p-group, quaternion, upper-central, and solvability statements are examples/equivalences.

The core takes a subset A and defines the intersection of all normal subgroups containing it, equivalently the subgroup generated by conjugates. Subset and intersection-of-subgroups were added alongside group, normal-subgroup, and generated-subgroup.
The core defines H◁G by gHg⁻¹=H for every g, with G and H≤G as hypotheses. Group and subgroup are the direct defining inputs; coset, quotient, and conjugation references are explanatory consequences.
The criterion assumes G and N≤G and concludes normality exactly when gng⁻¹∈N. Group, subgroup, and normal-subgroup provide the stated hypotheses and output.
The core defines N_G(H)={g:gHg⁻¹=H} and proves it is a subgroup containing H. Group and subgroup supply the ambient operation and H; normality appears only as an equivalent interpretation.
Given a group action, the core defines G·x={g·x:g∈G}⊂X. Group-action is the direct prerequisite; partition and stabilizer are later consequences.
The lemma assumes a group acting on a set and concludes its distinct orbits partition X. Group, set, orbit, and partition correspond exactly to the hypotheses and output.

For finite G, the theorem defines ord(g) as least n with gⁿ=e and concludes ord(g)| |G|. The only defining ambient input is a finite group; cyclic-subgroup and Lagrange are explanatory equivalent/corollary links.

The definition combines an abelian group with a translation-invariant total order. Abelian-group and total-order directly provide both structures; positive-cone details are equivalent characterization prose.
A p-group is defined by element orders p^k, equivalently finite cardinality p^n. Group and cardinality supply the two formulations; center and Sylow links are later remarks.
The theorem assumes a finite p-group of order p^n with n≥1 and concludes its center has size divisible by p. P-group and center are the exact hypothesis/output concepts.
The corollary states p|Z(G)| for a finite p-group and illustrates D₈. P-group and center directly supply the hypothesis and conclusion; the class-equation proof is a remark.
The proposition assumes a finite p-group |G|=p^n and concludes a subgroup of every order p^k, including k=0,n. P-group and subgroup match the structural hypothesis and output.
The definition is [G,G]=G, with commutator-subgroup supplying the derived subgroup and group the ambient object. Abelian/simple consequences are examples/equivalences.
The definition is a homomorphism G→Sym(X), equivalently an action, with Sym(X) consisting of bijections. Group, group-homomorphism, bijective-function, and group-action are all direct ingredients.

The theorem defines determinant modulo nth powers on PGL and identifies kernel PSL in a short exact sequence. Projective groups, determinant, and exact-sequence targets support each displayed term and the field-specific examples.
A finite group of prime order has every nonidentity element generate G. Group is the direct hypothesis; Lagrange and cyclic-subgroup occur only in context/conclusion notation.
The proposition assumes two normal subgroups and proves NM=MN and normality using conjugation. Group and normal-subgroup are the exact inputs to the displayed set and proof.
PGL(V)=GL(V)/(k×I) requires a nonzero finite-dimensional vector space, the general linear group, and quotient group. The projective-space action and PSL comparison are later sections.
The definition quantifies powers g^n=e and concludes g=e, so group is the only prerequisite. Free groups appear as an example of torsion-free groups, not a defining input.
